DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 20SMCV01985    Hearing Date: September 2, 2026    Dept: 205

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

WCO SPECTRUM, LLC,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

SIGNAL FLARE CAPITAL INC., et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 20SMCV01985 

 

  Hearing Date: September 2, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  PLAINTIFF AND CROSS-DEFENDANTS’  

  MOTIONS FOR ATTORNEYS’ FEES,  

  EXPERT FEES AND COSTS and  

  defendant and cross- 

  complainants’ motion to tax  

  costs 

 

BACKGROUND 

This action arises from a dispute between alleged partners.  Plaintiff WCO Spectrum LLC filed this action against Defendant Lee Stein, alleging that Mr. Stein misappropriated WCO’s confidential business information, trade secrets, and proprietary strategies. WCO claimed that Mr. Stein obtained confidential information in his role as WCO’s potential attorney to create a competing business, Defendant Signal Flare Capital Inc.  Mr. Stein countersued, alleging that he and Cross-Defendant Gary Winnick had entered into an oral partnership agreement to “pursue business opportunities and projects together” and to share profits and losses 50/50.  

On August 3, 2021, the Winnick Parties served Request for Admission No. 1, Set One, asking Mr. Stein to admit that he “never entered into the PARTNERSHIP with WINNICK” — a term defined by reference to the partnership Stein alleged was formed on April 25, 2019. [Ex. 3 to Sugden Decl.].  Mr. Stein denied the request on September 14, 2021. [Id.] 

On October 15, 2024, the Winnick Parties served a written offer to compromise Stein’s Cross-Complaint under Code of Civil Procedure section 998.  That Offer read, in pertinent part, that the Winnick Parties “offer to have a judgment entered in Cross-Defendants’ favor, and against Cross-Complainant Lee Stein (“Cross-Complainant”) as to Cross-Complainant’s Cross-Complaint in this action, for the sum of two-hundred fifty thousand dollars ($250,000.00) ….” [Ex. 18 to Sugden Decl.]. Stein did not accept. 

 

On November 20, 2025, the jury returned a unanimous verdict. The Special Verdict Form asked: “Question 1. In April 2019, did Lee Stein and Gary Winnick orally form a partnership to split profits 50/50 on any opportunity they explored?” The jury unanimously answered: “No”. (Ex. 8 to Sugden Decl..) The jury’s finding that no partnership existed between Mr. Stein and Mr. Winnick established the very matter that Mr. Stein had refused to admit in response to RFA No. 1: that Mr. Stein “never entered into the PARTNERSHIP with WINNICK.”  

On April 21, 2026, this Court entered judgment confirming the jury’s verdict, ordering that Lee Stein “shall take nothing from WCO Spectrum, LLC and Gary Winnick (Deceased) by way of his crossclaims.” The Court further noted that it “reserves the ability to amend this judgment to reflect the award of additional relief as may be sought by the Parties.” (Ex. 9 to Sugden Decl.) 

This hearing is on the Winnick Parties’ motions for attorney’s fees, expert fees and costs.  The Winnick Parties seek $1,169,994.80 in attorneys’ fees and $304,657.39 in discretionary costs and expert fees.  They argue that under Code Civ. Proc. section 2033.420, they are entitled to fees and costs because Mr. Stein failed to admit a matter which they later proved to be true, and Mr. Stein had no reasonable grounds for denying the request for admission.  They also argue that they are entitled to reasonable costs as the prevailing party under section 1032(b) because the Court entered judgment in their favor and against Mr. Stein on all causes of action in his cross-complaint.  Additionally, the Winnick Parties argue that because they made an offer to compromise in the amount of $250,000 and Mr. Stein failed to obtain a more favorable judgment – indeed he obtained nothing—the Winnick Parties are entitled to recover their post-offer expert witness fees and costs pursuant to section 998(d). 

This hearing is also on Mr. Stein’s motion to tax costs.  Mr. Stein seeks to tax costs enumerated in the Winnick Parties’ memorandum of costs (totaling $170,827.23).  Mr. Stein argues that the Winnick Parties are not entitled to costs under section 1032 because they are not the prevailing party under California law.  In opposition, the Winnick Parties argue that even if they are not the prevailing party, they are entitled to costs under sections 998 and 2033.420.   

DISCUSSION   

Section 2033.420 

The Winnick Parties seek attorneys’ fees and costs pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section¿2033.420, subdivision (a)¿which provides that a party may seek the reasonable expenses including attorney fees of proving the truth of the matter in an RFA that was denied by a responding party. 

An award of such expenses is mandatory unless the court finds one of the following: (1) an objection to the request was sustained or a response to it was waived under Section 2033.290; (2) the admission sought was of no substantial importance; (3) the party failing to make the admission had reasonable ground¿to believe that that party would prevail on the matter; and (4) there was other good reason for the failure to admit.  (Code Civ. Proc., § 2033.420, subd. (b).)  The burden for justifying the denial of the RFAs pursuant to any one of these four exceptions falls on the responding party. (Samsky v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Ins. Co. (2019) 37 Cal.App.5th 517, 523-524.) 

As a threshold matter, the Court must decide whether the RFA covers the exact same issue as the jury finding.  The RFA asks: “Admit that YOU never entered into the PARTNERSHIP with WINNICK.”  Meanwhile, the jury answered “no” to the following question: “In April 2019, did Lee Stein and Gary Winnick orally form a partnership to split profits 50/50 on any opportunity they explored?” 

Mr. Stein argues that the RFA sought a broader admission than what the jury ultimately found.  The RFA referred to a “PARTNERSHIP”, whereas the jury found there was no partnership to split profits 50/50.  In reply, the Winnick Parties argue that the RFA “asked [Mr. Stein] to admit he never entered the very partnership he had pleaded, formed by handshake in a limousine on April 25, 2019, under which he and Winnick would “jointly own and control the partnership and … share profits and losses.’”   

Surprisingly, the Winnick Parties never submit a copy of the RFA which would shed light on how “PARTNERSHIP” was defined in the RFA and whether in fact there is no daylight between the RFA and the jury finding.  The Court only has the response to the RFA which does not indicate how “PARTNERSHIP” is defined in the RFA.  Under¿section¿2033.420,¿subdivision (a), the party seeking an award of reasonable expenses has the¿initial¿burden¿of establishing “that it actually proved the matter” covered by the request for admission.¿(1 Hogan & Weber, Cal. Civil Discovery (2d ed. 2018 Supp.)  Accordingly, the Court concludes that the Winnick Parties have not met their burden.  

Even assuming the Court accepts the Winnick Parties’ representation that they defined “PARTNERSHIP” based on the allegations in the Cross-Complaint, the Cross-Complaint referred to many other things that were purportedly agreed to as part of the alleged partnership agreement, including that the parties would pursue business opportunities together and jointly control the partnership.  Accordingly, even accepting the Winnick Parties’ position, it would still not establish that the jury finding (of no partnership to split profits equally) and the fact sought to be admitted in the RFA are one and the same.  Therefore, the Court denies the section 2033.420 motion for attorneys’ fees.  

Section 1032(b) 

The Winnick Parties seek costs pursuant to section 1032(b).  Section 1032(b) allows a prevailing party to recover allowable costs as a matter of right.  In opposition, Mr. Stein argues that he is the prevailing party because he is the original defendant and the Winnick Parties got nothing.  The Court agrees with Mr. Stein.   

In general, the “prevailing party” is entitled as a matter of right to recover costs for suit in any action or proceeding. (Code Civ. Proc., §¿1032(b);¿Santisas v. Goodin (1998) 17 Cal.4th 599, 606;¿Scott Co. Of Calif, v. Blount, Inc. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 1103, 1108.) “Prevailing party” includes the party with a net monetary recovery, a defendant in whose favor a dismissal is entered, a defendant where neither plaintiff nor defendant obtains any relief, and a defendant as against those plaintiffs who do not recover any relief against that defendant.¿(Code Civ. Proc., § 1032 (a)(4).) 

In a situation where the defendant has filed a cross-complaint on which he has not prevailed, the California Court of Appeal has held that the defendant is still the prevailing party if the plaintiff obtained no relief.  (McLarand, Vasquez & Partners, Inc. (1991) 231 Cal.App.3d 1450, 1454).  There, the Court held that section 1032 “contemplates that when neither the plaintiff nor the defendant who has filed a cross-complaint prevails, the defendant is the prevailing party entitled to costs.”  (Id.) 

The Winnick Parties unsuccessfully attempt to distinguish McLarand.  The Winnick Parties argue that McLarand did not involve a section 998 offer or address section 2033.420.  But so what?  McLarand addresses the definition of prevailing party where a movant is seeking section 1032 costs, which is precisely what the Winnick Parties are doing here.  That there may be alternative grounds for their request for costs doesn’t mean that they can’t recover under section 1032.   

The Winnick Parties also argue that the economic realities differ because WCO’s own claims sought roughly $8,000 while Mr. Stein’s cross-claims sought far more ($7.5 million to $20 million). [Opp. at 12]. But the holding in McLarand does not turn on the relative dollar value of the competing claims.  Instead, it was based on a reading of the plain language in section 1032(a)(4), which does not allow the Court to engage in a relative claim value analysis to determine the identity of the prevailing party.  Further, WCO original Complaint sought no less than $100,000,000 in damages, which is far greater than the upper end of Mr. Stein’s claimed damages.   

The Winnick Parties further argue that its own claims were resolved by nonsuit mid-trial rather than by a contested verdict. [Opp. at 12-13]. McLarand rejected that same distinction. A nonsuit is a decision on the merits: the party against whom it is entered failed to make out a case the jury could decide. Nothing in section 1032(a)(4) or McLarand distinguishes a claim lost on nonsuit from a claim lost after a verdict. Both leave the party who brought the claim with no relief.  

The Winnick Parties also argue that “[c]ost-of-proof expenses do not turn on who prevailed. They turn on whether a party denied a matter without reasonable grounds and thereby put an opponent to the expense of proving it.”  But the Winnick Parties sought costs pursuant to section 1032(b), as well as section 2033.420.  Their reply suggests that they have now reversed course and no longer seek costs pursuant to 1032(b).  Regardless, as the Winnick Parties are not the prevailing party, they are not entitled to costs under section 1032. 

Section 998(d) 

The Winnick Parties seek post-offer costs pursuant to section 998(d).  Under section 998, a plaintiff (or in this case a cross-plaintiff) who fails to accept an offer and then fails to obtain a more favorable result at trial must pay the other party’s costs from the time of the offer. (Code Civ. Proc., § 998, subd. (c)(1).)  In opposition, Mr. Stein argues that he did obtain a more favorable result because the 998 offer required him to pay the Winnick Parties $250,000 while the Winnick Parties actually took nothing.  The Court agrees with Mr. Stein.   

The 998 Offer states that the Winnick Parties “offer to have a judgment entered in Cross Defendants’ favor, and against Cross-Complainant Lee Stein ... as to Cross-Complainant’s Cross Complaint in this action, for the sum of two-hundred fifty thousand dollars ($250,000.00).” [Ex. 18 to Sugden Decl.].  The Offer does not state that the Winnick Parties will pay Mr. Stein $250,000.  It states the opposite: that judgment may be entered “in Cross-Defendants’ favor, and against Cross-Complainant Lee Stein... for the sum of $250,000.” On its face, that language describes a $250,000 judgment against Stein — the reverse of how the Winnick Parties now characterize the Offer.  

Had Stein accepted, he would have had to pay $250,000 to the Winnick Parties. He did not accept, and the Judgment entered on April 21, 2026 requires him to pay nothing. [Ex. 8 to Sugden Decl.] A judgment requiring Stein to pay nothing is more favorable than a judgment requiring him to pay $250,000.  Mr. Stein therefore obtained a more favorable judgment than the Offer, and he is not obligated to pay the Winnick Parties’ post-offer costs.   

The Winnick Parties argue that Mr. Stein is misreading the 998 offer, and that read as a whole the Offer makes clear that payment was to be made by the Winnick Parties to Mr. Stein.  The Winnick Parties cite to paragraphs (A)-(C) of the Offer.  But nothing in those sections suggests that the $250,000 was to be paid to Mr. Stein.  There is not even any ambiguity in the Offer as to who is obligated to make the payment.  In any event, even if there was some uncertainty, we are bound to interpret the ambiguity against the Winnick Parties who drafted the 998 offer.  (Ignacio v. Caracciolo¿(2016) 2 Cal.App.5th 81, 86.) 

Motion to Tax Costs 

Mr. Stein moves to tax costs in the Winnick Parties’ memorandum of costs.  The issues raised in the motion to tax costs are virtually identical to those addressed above.   

The Winnick Parties filed a form memorandum of costs.  That form refers to sections 1032, 1033.5 and Rule of Court 3.1700(a).  All of those sections relate to an award of costs to a prevailing party.  Section 1032 provides that a prevailing party is entitled to seek costs.  Section 1033.5 lists the allowable costs.  And Rule 3.1700 governs how a prevailing party claims allowable litigation costs and how the opposing party may challenge them.  As set forth above, however, the Winnick Parties are not the prevailing party under McLarand and therefore, they cannot recover costs under the prevailing party costs statutes. 

In opposition to the motion to tax costs, the Winnick Parties point to alternative grounds to seek costs (under sections 998 and 2033.420).  As to section 998, it is true that such costs may be sought in a cost bill, and there is no rule requiring a noticed motion.  (Code Civ. Proc., §¿998, subd. (c)(1),¿(e);¿Thompson v. Miller¿(2003) 112 Cal.App.4th 327;¿Santantonio v. Westinghouse Broadcasting Co.¿(1994) 25 Cal.App.4th 102, 109–110.)  However, as stated above, the Court concludes that Mr. Stein obtained a more favorable result than the 998 offer because the offer required him to pay $250,000 and he ended up having to pay nothing.   

As to section 2033.420, it contemplates that the requesting party may “move” the Court for an order requiring the other party to pay costs associated with having to prove a matter denied in an RFA.  The statute, therefore, contemplates a motion, not a memorandum of costs.  In any event, it is clear from the memorandum of costs that it is not limited to 2033.420 costs.  It seeks costs from the inception of the action rather than from the point of Mr. Stein’s denial of the partnership RFA.  In any event, as discussed above, the Court concludes that Mr. Stein is not entitled to costs under section 2033.420. 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court DENIES the Winnick Parties’ motions for attorneys’ fees, expert fees, and costs and GRANTS Stein’s motion to tax costs.

Edward B. Moreton, Jr. 

Judge of the Superior Court 

Case Number: 26SMCV02748    Hearing Date: September 2, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

ADANY SANCHEZ,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

UBER TECHNOLOGIES, INC., et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  26SMCV02748  

  Hearing Date: September 2, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  defendant OSVALDO DEL REAL’S  

  motion to stay civil proceedings  

  pending resolution of related  

  criminal matter 

  

 

  

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a negligence and negligent hiring case.  On May 3, 2026, Defendant Osvaldo Del Real (erroneously sued as Del Rio) drove his car into Plaintiff Adany Sanchez’s car. (FAC ¶¶ 1, 5.) Plaintiff alleges that a few hours earlier, Del Real struck a deputy with the Los Angeles Sheriff’s Department during a traffic stop and fled the scene. (Id. at ¶ 3.)  

Later that day, Plaintiff alleges that Del Real accessed the Uber platform and picked up a passenger.  While he was driving the passenger, police identified his car and attempted to initiate a traffic stop. (Id. at ¶ 4.) Plaintiff claims that Del Real attempted to evade the police, and during the course of that pursuit, collided with Plaintiff’s car. (Id. at ¶¶ 5-6.)  Del Real also held his Uber passenger hostage for hours until he was ultimately arrested.  (Id. at ¶ 7.) 

Plaintiff has sued Del Real and various Uber entities.  The operative complaint alleges claims for (1) negligence and (2) negligent hiring, training, supervision and retention.   

Del Real has been criminally charged in the Los Angeles Superior Court, case number 26IWCF00276-01, with “Assault With Deadly Weapon not a Firearm on P.O./Firefighter: Great Bodily Injury Likely (Count 001), Evading Police Officer: Disregard Safety (Count 002), False Imprisonment of a Hostage (Count 003), Possess Controlled Substance While Armed With Loaded Firearm (Count 004), Possess Controlled Substance While Armed With Loaded Firearm (Count 005), and Possession of Unmarked Firearm (Count 006, 007, and 008)” on May 3, 2026. (Chrun Decl., ¶ 4.) 

This hearing is on Del Real’s motion to stay civil proceedings pending resolution of related criminal matter.  Del Real argues that the parallel criminal action will compel him to assert the Fifth Amendment privilege against self incrimination in this case and thereby allow Plaintiff to prevail on the merits.  Accordingly, a stay is necessary in order to avoid forcing Del Real to defend the actions on two fronts, thereby ensuring his inability to fully defend any action to the fullest extent possible.  In the alternative, Del Real seeks a stay of discovery against him.  Uber has joined in Del Real’s motion for a stay. 

LEGAL STANDARD 

Trial courts have the inherent power to make orders that will provide for the orderly conduct of proceedings before it and to amend and control its process and orders so as to conform to law and justice. (Code Civ. Proc. §§ 128(a),¿187.)  On this basis, trial courts may stay proceedings “in the interests of justice and to promote judicial efficiency.” (Freiberg v. City of Mission Viejo (1995) 33 Cal.App.4th 1484, 1489.)   

This discretion allows trial courts to stay discovery, or to stay the¿entire case, pending resolution of parallel criminal proceedings.¿(Avant! Corp v. Superior Court¿(2000) 79 Cal.App.4th 876, 887¿(trial courts have discretion to consider whether to stay civil proceedings pending completion of parallel criminal proceedings);¿County of Orange v. Superior Court¿(2000) 79 Cal.App.4th 759, 768-69¿(trial court has discretion to consider whether to stay civil proceedings, and related discovery, pending completion of parallel criminal proceedings);¿Pacers, Inc. v. Superior Court¿(1984) 162 Cal.App.3d 686, 690 (trial court has discretion to consider whether to stay civil discovery pending completion of parallel criminal proceedings).) 

DISCUSSION 

The “Constitution does not ordinarily¿require a stay of civil proceedings pending the outcome of¿criminal¿proceedings.” (Keating v. Office of Thrift Supervision¿(9th Cir. 1995) 45 F.3d 322, 324.) “In the absence of substantial¿prejudice¿to the rights of the parties involved, parallel proceedings are unobjectionable under our jurisprudence… Nevertheless, a court may decide in its discretion to¿stay¿civil¿proceedings¿when the interests of justice seem to require such action." (Id.¿at 324.)¿ 

In determining whether to stay civil proceedings pending completion of parallel criminal proceedings, the Court considers: “(1) the interest of the plaintiffs in proceeding expeditiously with this litigation or any particular aspect of it, and the potential prejudice to plaintiffs of a delay; (2) the burden which any particular aspect of the proceedings may impose on defendants; (3) the convenience of the court in the management of its cases, and the efficient use of judicial resources; (4) the interests of persons not parties to the civil litigation; and (5) the interest of the¿public in the pending civil¿and criminal litigation.” (Avant!, supra, 79 Cal.App.4th at¿887).) 

The Court concludes that the Avant! factors support a stay of the proceedings.  The burden on Del Real is clear.  He is subject to pending criminal proceedings based on the exact set of circumstances at issue in this case.  He will be severely prejudiced if the civil action proceeds because civil discovery is broader than criminal discovery and could potentially expose his criminal defense to the prosecution.   

Also, Plaintiff will not be prejudiced because the evidence in the criminal case will be preserved.¿ The accident occurred only four months ago (in May 2026), and there is no indication that witnesses’ memories will fade or evidence will be destroyed particularly given the pending criminal investigation.  Further, staying the civil action will not hinder judicial efficiency because a potential criminal verdict could automatically establish Del Real’s liability in this action and thereby, eliminate unnecessary discovery or motion practice.  The Court can also re-evaluate whether the stay should continue based on developments in the criminal proceedings. 

Additionally, there are no interests of any persons not parties to this action that will be impacted.  Finally, public interest weighs in favor of a stay.  Courts have recognized the public interest in ensuring that the¿integrity¿of the¿criminal¿process is not subverted, some stating that such interest is entitled to precedence over the interests of a¿civil¿litigant.  (See, e.g.,¿State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Healthcare Chiropractic Clinic, Inc., 2016 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 195186, 2016 WL 9307608, at *6 (D. Minn. Apr. 26, 2016);¿Gerhardt, 2007 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 35481, 2007 WL 1452236, at *2.)   

Plaintiff argues that the overlap between this action and the pending criminal proceeding is minimal because the criminal proceeding concerns additional issues relating to “firearms, controlled substances, alleged kidnapping/false imprisonment, and conduct toward law enforcement” while this case involves Del Real’s negligent operation of a car.  (Opp. at 3-4.)  But Plaintiff’s own complaint proves otherwise.  But the FAC is riddled with allegations concerning Del Real’s hitting the police, his fleeing from the police, and his kidnapping of an Uber passenger (FAC ¶¶ 3-8, 29-31, 42, 38, 50)—and Plaintiff relies on that same conduct as a basis for her claims against the Uber Defendants.  

Plaintiff argues that Del Real can simply invoke his Fifth Amendment privilege on a question-by question basis, and that the Court can resolve any resulting privilege disputes as they arise. (Opp. at p. 5.)  Not true.  “[I]n the criminal context, a defendant may not selectively invoke the Fifth Amendment to avoid cross-examination.” (Doe v. Regents of Univ. of Cal. (2016) 5 Cal.App.5th 1055, 1100, collecting cases.) Setting aside that the law does not permit selective invocation of the Fifth Amendment, Plaintiff’s proposed solution would still require Del Real to choose between invoking his Fifth Amendment privilege or providing testimony concerning conduct implicated in his pending criminal prosecution. 

Plaintiff also argues that she will suffer prejudice because “witness memories fade, witnesses become unavailable, and electronic evidence including video, GPS, cellular, vehicle, and app-based records may be lost or overwritten.”  But Plaintiff has not identified any witnesses beyond herself, Del Real and the Uber passenger.  All three are witnesses in the criminal case whose recollections would be preserved in the criminal action.  As to evidence regarding video, GPS, cellular, vehicle and app-based records, these are electronic documents that are not likely to be destroyed.  Surely, the police would not overwrite or lose the evidence they need for the criminal prosecution.  Further, as Defendants have notice of the litigation, they are required to preserve evidence, or risk claims of spoliation and attendant sanctions related to same.   

Plaintiff next argues that discovery against the Uber Defendants can proceed “independently” because they do not share Del Real’s Fifth Amendment privilege. (Opp. at 4-7.) To be sure, Plaintiff’s discovery against Uber would not implicate Del Real’s Fifth Amendment privilege.  But discovery goes both ways, and the Uber Defendants would be entitled to get discovery from Plaintiff as well, which would potentially mean that Plaintiff would have to sit for deposition twice.  Also, the discovery that either party seeks would be impacted by information from Del Real, which cannot be provided until the criminal proceeding concludes.  The scope of permissible discovery would also be impacted by information from Del Real, which will make it difficult for either the Uber Defendants or the Court to decide whether Plaintiff’s discovery requests are relevant or reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence.  All of this would create fragmented discovery and significant inefficiencies.   

In sum, the Court concludes that all of the Avant! factors weigh in favor of staying the entire proceedings. 

CONCLUSION 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS Defendants’ motion to stay the civil proceedings pending resolution of the criminal matter.  The Court sets a Status Conference re Stay Pending Resolution of Criminal Proceedings on June 3, 2027 at 8:30 a.m. 

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.
